documents.title: Academic Integrity (Undergraduate Catalog)
documents.summary: The undergraduate catalog academic-integrity policy defines misconduct, with unauthorized AI use and uses of generative AI without explicit instructor permission counted as dishonesty. It lays out sanctions, reporting to the Provost, and a multi-step appeal process; AI appears only in the misconduct definitions.
documents.stance_why: The definitions list "artificial intelligence, etc. without instructor’s permission" and "generative AI tools ... without explicit permission from the instructor" as dishonesty, so AI is barred unless the instructor permits it, which is restrict.

units.why: The principles state that "Academic dishonesty is prohibited in all programs of the university", a general integrity rule that frames the later AI provisions; coded as a fairness/honesty rationale (P95) because it grounds the rules in "honesty, trust, fairness" rather than skill-building.
units.anchor: shared culture of honesty, trust, fairness, respect, and responsibility

units.why: "Students are responsible for the honest completion and representation of their work" binds students to own what they submit, so P29 (own everything submitted).
units.anchor: Students are responsible for the honest completion and representation of their work

units.why: This bullet lists "artificial intelligence" among unauthorized materials "without instructor’s permission", making AI banned unless the instructor permits it. I chose P06 (default when permission is absent) over P36 because the distinctive content is the permission-based default; the misconduct label is coded in the next unit.
units.anchor: artificial intelligence, etc. without instructor’s permission
units.fit_note: Applies to all unauthorized materials (online sources, devices, social media, AI), not to AI alone.

units.why: The definition classes unauthorized materials, including AI, as "Academic dishonesty ... subject to disciplinary action", so unauthorized AI use is misconduct handled by integrity processes (P36).
units.anchor: Academic Dishonesty and Misconduct Subject to Disciplinary Action

units.why: The policy defines as dishonesty using "generative AI tools, such as chatbots, image generators, or code generators" for academic work "without explicit permission from the instructor", which classifies unauthorized generative AI as misconduct (P36) and sets an explicit-permission default.
units.anchor: without explicit permission from the instructor
units.fit_note: Also sets the default that AI needs explicit instructor permission (P06); one unit, one type.

units.why: The sentence names "entering assignment or exam questions into AI tools to generate answers" as misuse, which matches P20 (do not feed assignment questions to AI).
units.anchor: entering assignment or exam questions into AI tools to generate answers

units.why: "Submitting AI-generated content as original work" is listed as misuse, i.e. AI may not produce the work a student submits as their own (P19).
units.anchor: submitting AI-generated content as original work

units.why: "Failing to disclose the use of AI in creating submissions when required" makes nondisclosure itself a violation, which is P28 (nondisclosure is the violation) rather than P24 since it frames the consequence.
units.anchor: failing to disclose the use of AI in creating submissions when required

units.why: Sanctions "may be imposed by an instructor for academic misconduct" are listed (repeat the work, lower or failing grade); these are concrete penalties (P37), applied to AI misuse as part of misconduct.
units.anchor: A lower or failing grade on the assignment or test
units.frag_end: A failing grade in the course
units.fit_note: Penalties apply to all academic misconduct, not specifically to AI.

units.why: For "egregious or repeated incidences" the instructor, dean or provost may impose an FX, suspension or expulsion, an escalation of penalties by offense (P37).
units.anchor: Permanent expulsion from the university
units.fit_note: General misconduct sanctions, not AI-specific.

units.why: "The student may not withdraw from the course to avoid the sanction" fixes a consequence in advance (P37), so a final-grade sanction cannot be escaped by withdrawing.
units.anchor: the student may not withdraw from the course to avoid the sanction
units.fit_note: General misconduct rule.

units.why: "Unintentional errors ... may be addressed through educational remedies" when there is no intent, which is an educative rather than punitive response (P68), although the examples are citation or collaboration mistakes not AI.
units.anchor: may be addressed through educational remedies
units.fit_note: Examples given are citation and collaboration mistakes; AI is not named.

units.why: Before sanctioning, "the instructor shall notify the student that the instructor believes an act of academic misconduct has occurred", i.e. the student is told before escalation (P57).
units.anchor: the instructor shall notify the student that the instructor believes an act of academic misconduct
units.frag_end: with the Office of the Provost.
units.fit_note: Notification rather than gathering context from the student; general misconduct rule.

units.why: "Instructors are encouraged to engage students in a discussion of the importance of academic integrity and why the instructor considers a sanction appropriate" is an educative conversation (P68) rather than a pure penalty.
units.anchor: encouraged to engage students in a discussion of the importance of academic integrity
units.fit_note: Discussion is of integrity generally, not AI rules.

units.why: Instructors must notify the Provost "no later than ten days after the infraction is discovered" using a required form, a formal reporting procedure (P81).
units.anchor: no later than ten days after the infraction is discovered

units.why: "Instructors should file a notification of academic dishonesty regardless of the severity" extends the formal reporting duty to every case (P81).
units.anchor: Instructors should file a notification of academic dishonesty regardless of the severity

units.why: The Provost must give the student notice including "the student’s right to and process for an appeal", giving the accused a route to respond (P64).
units.anchor: indicating the student’s right to and process for an appeal

units.why: "A student who receives notice ... has the right to a hearing before the academic dean to contest that academic misconduct occurred", a right to respond (P64).
units.anchor: has the right to a hearing before the academic dean

units.why: The dean’s conference is designed "to afford the student an opportunity to respond", a fairness step in integrity cases (P64).
units.anchor: afford the student an opportunity to respond

units.why: "A finding of misconduct must be based on a preponderance of the credible evidence" sets the standard of proof (P69).
units.anchor: A finding of misconduct must be based on a preponderance of the credible evidence

units.why: A further appeal to the Provost is allowed only on due-process grounds such as "bias by the instructor or dean", guaranteeing procedural fairness (P64).
units.anchor: Evidence that bias by the instructor or dean substantially influenced the outcome
units.fit_note: Grounds for appeal rather than a right to respond; closest type.

units.why: The Academic Integrity Appeals Board is described as "an ad hoc committee appointed by the provost", naming who hears and decides appeals, which is P80.
units.anchor: ad hoc committee appointed by the provost
units.frag_start: The Academic Integrity Appeals Board is
units.frag_end: in the event of a tie.

units.why: "The student shall have the right to be heard and to present relevant evidence" at the Board hearing is a right to respond to allegations (P64).
units.anchor: The student shall have the right to be heard and to present relevant evidence
units.frag_start: The student shall have the right

documents.title: Artificial Intelligence in Syllabi
documents.summary: Teaching-center guidance giving four sample syllabus statements from restrictive to encouraging and strongly recommending, but not requiring, an AI statement. The university leaves the choice of rule to each instructor.
documents.stance_why: The page offers templates "ranging from restrictive to permissive" and says "Feel free to adapt the suggested language", and an AI statement is "not required", so the document sets no stance itself and delegates with tiers.

units.why: The page opens saying generative AI carries "great potential to reshape the way we teach, learn and engage with knowledge", a statement of AI benefits (P87), not a rule.
units.anchor: carry great potential to reshape the way we teach, learn and engage with knowledge

units.why: "faculty should clearly communicate their policies regarding the use of AI in their courses" asks instructors to state expectations to students (P09, with weaker force than a requirement).
units.anchor: faculty should clearly communicate their policies regarding the use of AI in their courses
units.fit_note: Recommendation to communicate policies; the next units state it is not required in the syllabus.

units.why: The page says "To ensure academic integrity, foster critical thinking skills and maintain a fair learning environment", giving fairness and integrity as the reason for stating policies (P95).
units.anchor: To ensure academic integrity, foster critical thinking skills and maintain a fair learning environment

units.why: "While faculty are not required to include an AI statement in their syllabi, it is strongly recommended" makes the syllabus statement optional but advised (P09 fits partly).
units.anchor: are not required to include an AI statement in their syllabi, it is strongly recommended
units.fit_note: The university does not require the statement; it only strongly recommends it.

units.why: The sample statements range "from restrictive to permissive approaches", offering a spread of positions the instructor can pick, i.e. named levels (P05).
units.anchor: ranging from restrictive to permissive approaches
units.fit_note: Four labeled example statements (Generic, Restrictive, Permissive, Permissive/Encouraging) rather than formal tiers.

units.why: "Feel free to adapt the suggested language for your specific class" leaves the AI rule to each instructor (P04).
units.anchor: Feel free to adapt the suggested language for your specific class

units.why: The guidance says the examples prioritize "the development of students’ authentic knowledge and skills", a skill-building rationale (P41).
units.anchor: prioritizing the development of students’ authentic knowledge and skills

units.why: Example 1 says AI use is "strictly prohibited unless explicitly stated otherwise", a default ban with instructor exceptions, matching P01 (and implying a fallback rule).
units.anchor: is strictly prohibited unless explicitly stated otherwise
units.fit_note: Ban applies "unless explicitly stated otherwise"; also acts as fallback (P06).

units.why: "Any permitted use of AI must be clearly declared ... detailing the AI tools used, the assistance received, and how this informed your final submission" requires tool, help and effect to be reported (P25).
units.anchor: detailing the AI tools used, the assistance received, and how this informed your final submission

units.why: Example 1 aims "to ensure that students engage personally with the learning process", fostering critical thinking: skill-building reason for the ban (P41).
units.anchor: students engage personally with the learning process

units.why: "Violations of this policy will be considered academic misconduct" classes the AI breach as misconduct handled under the Academic Integrity Policy (P36).
units.anchor: Violations of this policy will be considered academic misconduct

units.why: "Students are encouraged to ask any questions or seek clarifications about the use of AI technologies in this course" tells students to ask when unsure (P10).
units.anchor: encouraged to ask any questions or seek clarifications about the use of AI technologies

units.why: Example 2 states AI "is strictly prohibited in completing any coursework, assignments, quizzes, exams or any other form of assessment", a blanket default ban (P01).
units.anchor: strictly prohibited in completing any coursework, assignments, quizzes, exams or any other form of assessment
units.fit_note: Also covers exams and quizzes (P22); chosen P01 as the blanket course rule.

units.why: Example 2 says violations "will be considered academic misconduct" under the university procedures, classing misuse as misconduct (P36).
units.anchor: will be considered academic misconduct and will be subject to disciplinary actions

units.why: Example 2 justifies the ban to "maintain a fair and equitable learning environment", a fairness reason (P95).
units.anchor: maintain a fair and equitable learning environment

units.why: The ban also exists to encourage "critical thinking, problem-solving and academic writing skills without reliance on AI-generated content", a skill-building reason (P41).
units.anchor: critical thinking, problem-solving and academic writing skills without reliance on AI-generated content

units.why: Example 3 opens "AI can serve as a valuable resource for certain assignments", a conditional permission (P02 chosen as the default stance is allow).
units.anchor: AI can serve as a valuable resource for certain assignments
units.fit_note: Permission limited to "certain assignments", so partly instructor/assignment-specific (P04).

units.why: Students must "thoroughly assess and validate any information produced by AI", a duty to verify output (P31).
units.anchor: thoroughly assess and validate any information produced by AI

units.why: "The final submission must predominantly reflect the student’s original thought, analysis and synthesis" requires submitted work to be the student’s own (P29) even if AI informed it.
units.anchor: final submission must predominantly reflect the student’s original thought, analysis and synthesis

units.why: "All uses of GAI tools must be transparently cited, detailing the AI tools used, the assistance received" requires citation with tool and help details (P25).
units.anchor: All uses of GAI tools must be transparently cited

units.why: "Violations will be treated seriously, in line with the university’s Academic Integrity procedures" links misuse to the integrity process (P36).
units.anchor: Violations will be treated seriously, in line with the university’s

units.why: "please consult with the instructor for guidance" directs students who are unsure to ask the instructor (P10).
units.anchor: please consult with the instructor for guidance

units.why: Example 4 says "Students are encouraged to explore and utilize these tools responsibly", an encouraging default (P02).
units.anchor: Students are encouraged to explore and utilize these tools responsibly

units.why: The example says GAI tools "enhance learning experiences and foster creativity", a benefit claim (P87).
units.anchor: to enhance learning experiences and foster creativity

units.why: Students may "Use GAI tools for brainstorming, idea generation and preliminary research", an allowed use (P15).
units.anchor: Use GAI tools for brainstorming, idea generation and preliminary research

units.why: "Critically evaluate and independently verify the information generated by AI" is a duty to check output (P31).
units.anchor: Critically evaluate and independently verify the information generated by AI

units.why: "The final submission must demonstrate the student’s original thought, analysis and synthesis" repeats the own-work duty in the encouraging template (P29).
units.anchor: final submission must demonstrate the student’s original thought, analysis and synthesis

units.why: "All uses of GAI tools must be transparently cited, detailing the AI tools used, the assistance received" is the citation duty in Example 4 (P25).
units.anchor: All uses of GAI tools must be transparently cited

units.why: Example 4 closes "please consult with the instructor for guidance" on questions, so students ask when unsure (P10).
units.anchor: consult with the instructor for guidance

documents.title: Generative Artificial Intelligence Security and Privacy Policy, IT-5-136
documents.summary: Formal IT security and privacy policy for GenAI use by employees and students. It limits what data may enter public tools, requires vendor agreements, and assigns users responsibility for verifying output; it does not address coursework rules.
documents.stance_why: Non-public information "may only be entered into" GenAI under a binding agreement and "must not be entered into" free public tools, allowing AI only under narrow conditions, so restrict (about data, not coursework).

units.why: The policy says non-public information may be entered into GenAI "only when there is a legally binding agreement" reviewed through procurement, a data-protection rule with vetted tools (P50).
units.anchor: non-public information may only be entered into, uploaded to, analyzed or otherwise processed
units.frag_end: sensitivity of the type of information.

units.why: "Non-public University information and data must not be entered into ... free, public GenAI solutions" is an explicit ban on feeding confidential data to public tools (P50).
units.anchor: entered into, uploaded to, analyzed or otherwise processed by free, public GenAI solutions

units.why: The rule "applies both when using freestanding GenAI technology tools and when GenAI functionality has been integrated by vendors into other software products", covering embedded AI (P07).
units.anchor: when GenAI functionality has been integrated by vendors into other software products
units.fit_note: Covers vendor-integrated AI in software generally, not editors/IDEs specifically.

units.why: "All use of GenAI at the University must also comply with relevant contractual, legal, or regulatory obligations" requires following law and other university policies (P77).
units.anchor: must also comply with relevant contractual, legal, or regulatory obligations
units.frag_start: All use of GenAI at the University

units.why: "GenAI users at the University must take ultimate responsibility for content created with these tools", i.e. users own what they produce (P29).
units.anchor: must take ultimate responsibility for content created with these tools
units.fit_note: Addressed to all users, not only students submitting coursework.

units.why: Users "must understand and mitigate the risks" such as "hallucinations, bias, unintentional plagiarism", a duty to be aware of AI error (P31).
units.anchor: they must understand and mitigate the risks associated with them

units.why: "Exploring and benefiting from GenAI is in UMass Lowell’s interest" and GenAI offers "tremendous potential", stating the benefits of AI (P87).
units.anchor: GenAI technology offers tremendous potential to expand users’ capabilities, efficiency, and productivity

units.why: The University "expects members of its Workforce and student body ... to educate themselves about these concerns", a duty to stay informed (P102).
units.anchor: to educate themselves about these concerns

units.why: The scope says the policy "applies to the use of GenAI solutions by university Workforce and students", setting who it covers (P61).
units.anchor: applies to the use of GenAI solutions by university Workforce and students

units.why: The definition says GenAI covers tools that "generate new text, data, images, or video" including "the incorporation of GenAI into other common software", defining scope (P61).
units.anchor: artificial intelligence software tools that ingest large training datasets

units.why: "Public GenAI solutions ... are the free versions available to the public" and "not considered secure or permissible for use with non-public or sensitive data", defining public tools and why they are off-limits for sensitive data (P50).
units.anchor: they are not considered secure or permissible for use with non-public or sensitive data
units.frag_start: Public GenAI solutions for the purposes
units.fit_note: Definition that doubles as a data-handling rule.

units.why: The "AI Hallucinations" definition explains that GenAI may create content that is "factually incorrect, misleading or fabricated", a reminder that output is often wrong (P31).
units.anchor: content or information that is factually incorrect, misleading or fabricated

units.why: The definition warns GenAI content "may expose users to a heightened risk of committing Unintentional Plagiarism" because sources are unknowable; no existing type covers plagiarism risk from AI output.
units.anchor: heightened risk of committing Unintentional Plagiarism
units.frag_start: Because it can be impossible for a user

units.why: "only data that is classified Public ... may be entered into free public GenAI solutions" restricts what data may go to public tools (P50).
units.anchor: only data that is classified “Public”

units.why: Processing nonpublic data requires "a formal agreement with the AI solution provider established through the University’s procurement processes", i.e. institutional vendor review (P65).

units.frag_start: To process nonpublic University data using GenAI
